opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is that when you build on open source, competition is part of the deal from day one. Spark is an Apache project. Anyone can take it, run it, and offer it as a service, and many companies do. So the question was never whether people would compete with us on Spark; they would. The question was how we create the most value for the ecosystem and for ourselves at the same time.

Our view has always been that the pie matters more than the slice. If Spark becomes the de facto standard for large-scale data processing, that's good for everyone, including us. Partnering with large companies, even ones with competing offerings, helps grow that pie. It brings Spark to customers we'd never reach on our own, it validates the technology, and it creates more developers who know it. Those developers eventually show up looking for the best way to run it.

Then you have to be honest with yourself about where you win. We don't win by owning the code; the code is open. We win by being the people who understand it most deeply, by moving fastest, by building the best end-to-end platform around it, and by offering things like reliability, performance, security, and collaboration that enterprises really care about. If you can't win on that, no partnership strategy will save you. If you can, partnerships become an amplifier rather than a threat.

There is tension, of course. In some deals you're cooperating on one front and competing hard on another, which some call "coopetition." What helps is being clear about boundaries: what's shared, what's ours, and making sure the incentives line up so both sides actually benefit. And you have to keep investing in the open-source community itself, because that's the foundation. If you neglect it, you lose the trust that makes the whole model work.

So, in short: embrace the fact that others will compete, partner where it expands adoption, and make sure your own product is genuinely the best place to run the technology. That's the bet we made.

r001.rationale: The response says the company wins by building the best end-to-end platform and that partnerships amplify its position, supporting partnership with competitors through confidence in its product.

r002.rationale: The response does not say the company deserves to lose if another company builds a better Spark product.

r003.rationale: It says Spark becoming the de facto standard is good for everyone, including the company, and that broader adoption creates customers for its platform.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I've always thought about it, going back to the early days of Databricks, is that open source changes the calculus completely. Spark was open source from day one. We gave it to the Apache Software Foundation. So by definition, anyone could take it and build a product on it, and many did. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, IBM, all of them offered Spark in some form.

Now, you can look at that as a threat, and honestly, in the early days, a lot of people told us it was a mistake. Why would you give away the core technology and then try to build a company around it? But our view was that the alternative is worse. If you keep it closed, you don't get the adoption. And without the adoption, there's no ecosystem, no community, no reason for anyone to standardize on it. The value of Spark came precisely from the fact that it became the default. Every company that offered it, including our competitors, made the pie bigger.

So the question becomes, how do you capture value when everybody can offer the same thing? And the answer for us was, you have to be the best at it. You have the people who created it, you understand where it's going, you can move faster. That's not a permanent advantage, but it's a real one, and it forces you to keep innovating rather than relying on a moat that may not hold anyway.

On the partnership side specifically, we partnered very early with Microsoft, with Azure Databricks, and later with Amazon and Google. And yes, these companies also compete with us. But the customers are on those clouds. If you don't meet them there, somebody else will. So the way I think about it is, you don't ask whether a partner could compete with you. Almost everyone can. You ask whether the partnership makes the customer better off, and whether it makes the ecosystem bigger. If it does, you do it, and you accept that you'll compete in some areas and cooperate in others. That's just the reality of infrastructure software today.

And frankly, the thing that protects you is not the contract or the exclusivity. It's the pace at which you keep building. The day you stop being the best place to run the thing you created, no partnership structure is going to save you.

r001.rationale: The response says partnerships can make customers better off and grow the ecosystem, while continued innovation protects the company. It does not clearly present confidence in building the best Spark products as the basis for pursuing those partnerships.

r002.rationale: The response says Databricks must keep building to remain the best place to run Spark, but it does not say the company deserves to lose if another company builds a better product.

r003.rationale: The response says competitors offering Spark made the pie bigger, but it does not clearly state that Spark’s success will ultimately translate into success for Databricks.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at where your interests are aligned. A company may compete with you in one area, but there may be another area where working together benefits both of you and, more importantly, benefits the customer. Those things can coexist.

With Spark, growing the ecosystem creates opportunities for everyone. That doesn’t mean you won’t compete on products. You still have to build a better product and deliver value to customers. But I wouldn’t rule out a partnership just because the company could also be a competitor. I’d ask what we can accomplish together and be clear about where we cooperate and where we compete.

r001.rationale: The response says they still need to build a better product, but does not express confidence that they can build the best Spark products or make that confidence the basis for partnering.

r002.rationale: It does not say the company deserves to lose if another company builds a better Spark product.

r003.rationale: It says growing the Spark ecosystem creates opportunities for everyone, but does not state that Spark’s success will ultimately lead to success for Ion Stoica’s company.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the customer. Customers want Spark to work with the systems and platforms they already use, so partnering with those companies makes sense, even if there is some overlap in our products.

Of course, you have to be clear about where you collaborate and where you compete. But I don’t think those are mutually exclusive. We can work together to grow the ecosystem and make Spark more useful, and then compete on who delivers the best product and the best experience for customers.

r001.rationale: The response says the companies can compete on product and customer experience, but it does not express confidence that Ion Stoica’s company will build the best Spark products as a reason to partner.

r002.rationale: The response does not say Ion Stoica’s company deserves to lose if another company builds a better Spark product.

r003.rationale: The response says collaboration can grow the ecosystem and make Spark more useful, but does not say Spark’s success will translate into success for Ion Stoica’s company.
